chapters.title: The Old Sea-dog at the Admiral Benbow
paragraphs: It was Squire Trelawney, Dr. Livesey, and the rest of the gentlemen who asked me to write down the whole story of Treasure Island, beginning to end — to hold nothing back but where the island lies, and that only because there is treasure still buried there. So I take up my pen in the year 17—, and go back to when my father kept the Admiral Benbow inn, and the brown old seaman with the sabre scar across his face first came to lodge under our roof.

I remember him as if it were yesterday, plodding up to the inn door with his sea-chest hauled behind him on a barrow — a tall, strong, heavy man, nut-brown, his tarry pigtail hanging over the shoulder of a grubby blue coat, his hands cracked and scarred with black, broken nails, and that sabre scar across one cheek, a dirty, livid white. I can still see him glancing round the cove and whistling to himself, then suddenly breaking into the old sea-song he would sing so often afterward:
“Fifteen men on the dead man’s chest— Yo-ho-ho, and a bottle of rum!”

— in that high, cracked old voice that seemed to have been worn and broken at the capstan bars. Then he rapped on the door with a stick like a handspike that he carried, and when my father appeared he gruffly called for a glass of rum. When it came he drank it slowly, like a man who knew his liquor, lingering on the taste, his eyes still roving over the cliffs and up at our signboard.
“This is a handy cove,” he said at last, “and a pleasant spot for a tavern. Much custom, mate?”
My father told him no — very little, worse luck.

“Well then,” said he, “this is the berth for me. Here, matey,” he called to the man with the barrow, “bring her alongside and help up my chest. I’ll be staying a while,” he went on. “I’m a plain man — rum and bacon and eggs is what I want, and that headland up there to watch for ships. What to call me? You can call me captain. Oh, I see what you’re after — there.” And he flung three or four gold pieces down on the doorstep. “Tell me when I’ve drunk through that,” said he, with a look as fierce as any commander’s.

And indeed, ragged as his clothes were and rough as he talked, he looked nothing like a common hand who sailed before the mast — more like a mate or skipper used to being obeyed, or to hitting out. The man with the barrow told us the coach had set him down the morning before at the Royal George; that he had asked what inns there were along the coast; and that, hearing ours well spoken of and described as lonely, he had picked it over the rest for his lodging. That was all we ever learned about our guest.

He was a silent man by habit. All day he prowled the cove or the cliffs with a brass spyglass; all evening he sat in the corner of the parlour by the fire, drinking rum and water, very strong. Mostly he would not answer when spoken to — only glance up sharp and fierce and snort through his nose like a foghorn — and we and our regulars soon learned to leave him be. Every day, coming back from his walk, he would ask whether any seafaring men had passed along the road. At first we thought he asked for want of company of his own sort; in the end we saw it was the opposite — he wanted to avoid them. When a sailor did stop at the Admiral Benbow — as one did now and then, taking the coast road to Bristol — the captain would peer at him through the curtained door before coming into the parlour, and he was always quiet as a mouse while any such man was present. To me, at least, it was no mystery, for in a way I shared his fears. He had taken me aside one day and promised me a silver fourpenny on the first of every month if I would only keep my “weather-eye open for a seafaring man with one leg” and tell him the moment such a man appeared. Often enough, when the first of the month came round and I asked for my wages, he would only snort at me and stare me down; but before the week was out he was always sure to think better of it, bring me my fourpenny piece, and repeat his order to watch for “the seafaring man with one leg.”

I hardly need tell you how that figure haunted my dreams. On stormy nights, when the wind shook the four corners of the house and the surf roared in the cove and up the cliffs, I would see him in a thousand shapes, with a thousand devilish faces. Sometimes the leg was cut off at the knee, sometimes at the hip; sometimes he was a monstrous thing that had only ever had the one leg, set in the middle of his body. To watch him leap and run and chase me over hedge and ditch was the worst nightmare of all. So, one way and another, I paid pretty dear for my monthly fourpence, in the coin of these hideous dreams.

But frightened as I was by the idea of the one-legged sailor, I feared the captain himself far less than anyone else who knew him. There were nights he took more rum and water than his head could carry, and then he would sit singing his wicked old sea-songs, heeding nobody; but other nights he would call for drinks all round and force the whole trembling room to listen to his stories or join the chorus of his song. Many a time I have heard the house shaking with “Yo-ho-ho, and a bottle of rum,” every neighbour joining in for dear life, in terror, each singing louder than the next to escape notice. For in these fits he was the most overbearing company you ever saw: he would slap the table for silence; he would fly into a rage at a question, or at no question at all, deciding the company was not following his tale; and he would let no one leave the inn until he had drunk himself sleepy and staggered off to bed.

It was his stories that frightened people most. Dreadful stories — hangings, walking the plank, storms at sea, the Dry Tortugas, and wild deeds and places on the Spanish Main. By his own telling he must have spent his life among some of the wickedest men ever let loose on the ocean, and the language he told it in shocked our plain country folk almost as much as the crimes he described. My father was forever sure the inn would be ruined — that people would stop coming to be bullied and crushed and sent shivering to bed — but I really believe his presence did us good. People were frightened at the time, yet looking back they rather liked it; it was a fine bit of excitement in a quiet country life. There was even a knot of younger men who claimed to admire him, calling him a “true sea-dog” and a “real old salt” and the like, and saying it was men like him that made England feared at sea.

In one way, though, he did fairly threaten to ruin us, for he stayed on week after week, and then month after month, until the money he had put down was long gone, and still my father never plucked up the heart to insist on more. If ever he hinted at it, the captain snorted through his nose so loudly it was almost a roar, and stared my poor father out of the room. I have seen him wringing his hands after such a rebuff, and I am sure the worry and the fright he lived in did much to hasten his early and unhappy death.

All the while he lodged with us the captain never changed his clothes, except to buy a few stockings from a pedlar. One side of his hat-brim came down, and he let it hang from that day on, for all the bother it gave him in a wind. I remember his coat, which he patched himself upstairs in his room until, toward the end, it was nothing but patches. He never wrote a letter or got one, and he spoke to nobody but the neighbours — and to them, mostly, only when the rum was in him. The great sea-chest none of us had ever seen open.

He was crossed only once, and that was near the end, when my poor father was far gone in the decline that carried him off. Dr. Livesey came late one afternoon to see the patient, took a little dinner from my mother, and went into the parlour to smoke a pipe while he waited for his horse to be brought down from the hamlet — we had no stable at the old Benbow. I followed him in, and I remember the contrast: the neat, bright doctor, his hair powdered snow-white, his black eyes quick, his manner pleasant, against the clumsy country people, and above all against that filthy, hulking, bleary scarecrow of a pirate of ours, slumped far gone in rum with his arms on the table. Suddenly the captain struck up his everlasting song:
“Fifteen men on the dead man’s chest— Yo-ho-ho, and a bottle of rum! Drink and the devil had done for the rest— Yo-ho-ho, and a bottle of rum!”

At first I had taken “the dead man’s chest” to mean that very box of his upstairs in the front room, and the thought had got tangled in my nightmares with the one-legged sailor. But by now we had all long stopped paying the song any mind; that night it was new to no one but Dr. Livesey, and I could see it did not please him, for he glanced up a moment, quite angry, before going on with what he was saying to old Taylor the gardener about a new cure for rheumatism. Meanwhile the captain warmed to his own music, and at last slapped the table in the way we all knew meant silence. Every voice stopped at once — all but the doctor’s, who went on as before, clear and kind, drawing briskly at his pipe between every word or two. The captain glared at him a while, slapped the table again, glared harder, and at last burst out with a vile, low oath: “Silence, there, between decks!”

“Were you speaking to me, sir?” said the doctor; and when the ruffian, with another oath, told him he was, “I have only one thing to say to you, sir,” the doctor replied: “that if you keep on drinking rum, the world will soon be rid of a very dirty scoundrel.”
The old fellow’s fury was terrible. He sprang up, drew and snapped open a sailor’s clasp-knife, and, balancing it open on his palm, threatened to pin the doctor to the wall.

The doctor never so much as stirred. He spoke to him just as before, over his shoulder, in the same tone — pitched a little high, so the whole room could hear — perfectly calm and steady: “If you do not put that knife back in your pocket this instant, I promise you, on my honour, you shall hang at the next assizes.”
Then came a battle of looks between them, but the captain soon gave in, put away his weapon, and sat back down, growling like a beaten dog.

“And now, sir,” the doctor went on, “since I know there is such a man in my district, you may count on it that I shall keep an eye on you day and night. I am not a doctor only — I am a magistrate; and if I catch one breath of complaint against you, even for a rudeness like tonight’s, I shall see to it you are hunted down and turned out of here. Let that be enough.”
Soon after, Dr. Livesey’s horse came to the door and he rode away; but the captain held his tongue that evening, and for many evenings to come.

chapters.title: Black Dog Appears and Disappears
paragraphs: It was not long after this that the first of the strange events occurred — the ones that finally rid us of the captain, though not, as you will see, of his affairs. It was a bitter winter, with long hard frosts and heavy gales, and from the first it was plain my poor father had little chance of seeing the spring. He sank day by day, and my mother and I had the whole inn on our hands, busy enough without sparing much thought for our unwelcome guest.

It was early one January morning — a pinching, frosty morning — the cove all grey with hoar-frost, the ripples lapping softly on the stones, the sun still low and only touching the hilltops and shining far out to sea. The captain had risen earlier than usual and gone off down the beach, his cutlass swinging under the broad skirts of the old blue coat, his brass spyglass under his arm, his hat tilted back on his head. I remember his breath trailing like smoke behind him as he strode away, and the last sound I heard of him as he rounded the big rock was a loud, indignant snort, as though his mind were still running on Dr. Livesey.

Well, mother was upstairs with father, and I was laying the breakfast table for the captain’s return, when the parlour door opened and in stepped a man I had never set eyes on before. He was a pale, waxy creature, short two fingers on the left hand, and though he wore a cutlass he did not look much of a fighter. I always kept an eye out for seafaring men, one leg or two, and I remember this one puzzled me: he was not quite sailorly, and yet there was a smack of the sea about him all the same.
I asked what he would have, and he said rum; but as I went to fetch it he sat down on a table and waved me closer. I stopped where I was, napkin in hand.
“Come here, sonny,” said he. “Come a bit nearer.”
I took a step toward him.
“Is this table here set out for my mate Bill?” he asked, with a kind of leer.
I told him I knew no mate Bill — the table was for a man staying with us whom we called the captain.

“Well,” said he, “my mate Bill might well be called the captain, like as not. He has a cut on one cheek, and a mighty pleasant way with him, especially in drink, has my mate Bill. Let us say, for argument’s sake, that your captain has a cut on one cheek — and let us say, if you like, that it is the right cheek. Ah, there you are. Now — is my mate Bill in this house?”
I told him he was out walking.
“Which way, sonny? Which way is he gone?”

And when I had pointed out the rock, and told him how and how soon the captain was likely to be back, and answered a question or two more, “Ah,” said he, “this’ll be as good as a drink to my mate Bill.”

The look on his face as he said it was anything but pleasant, and I had my own reasons to think the stranger was mistaken, even if he meant what he said. But it was no business of mine, I thought, and besides it was hard to know what to do. The stranger kept lurking just inside the inn door, peering round the corner like a cat watching a mouse. Once I stepped out into the road myself, but he called me straight back, and when I did not move fast enough to suit him, a horrible change came over that waxy face and he ordered me in with an oath that made me jump. The moment I was back he turned smooth again, half fawning, half sneering, patted my shoulder and told me I was a good lad and he had taken quite a fancy to me. “I have a son of my own,” he said, “the very spit of you, and he is all the pride of my heart. But the great thing for boys is discipline, sonny — discipline. Now, if you had sailed with Bill, you’d not have stood there to be spoken to twice — not you. That was never Bill’s way, nor the way of them as sailed with him. And here, sure enough, is my mate Bill, with a spyglass under his arm, bless his old heart. You and me’ll just step back into the parlour, sonny, and get behind the door, and we’ll give Bill a little surprise — bless his heart, I say again.”

With that the stranger backed into the parlour with me and put me behind him in the corner, both of us hidden by the open door. I was very uneasy and alarmed, as you may imagine, and it did nothing for my nerves to see that the stranger was plainly frightened himself. He freed the hilt of his cutlass and loosened the blade in its sheath, and the whole time we waited he kept swallowing as if he had what we used to call a lump in the throat.
At last in strode the captain, slammed the door behind him without a glance to either side, and marched straight across the room to where his breakfast was waiting.
“Bill,” said the stranger, in a voice he seemed to force loud and bold.

The captain spun on his heel and faced us. All the brown had drained from his face; even his nose had gone blue. He had the look of a man seeing a ghost, or the devil, or something worse, if worse there is; and upon my word, I felt sorry to watch him turn, in a moment, so old and sick.
“Come, Bill — you know me; you know an old shipmate, surely, Bill,” said the stranger.
The captain gave a sort of gasp.
“Black Dog!” said he.

“And who else?” said the other, easier now. “Black Dog as ever was, come to see his old shipmate Billy at the Admiral Benbow inn. Ah, Bill, Bill, we have seen a deal of life, us two, since I lost these two talons,” — and he held up his maimed hand.
“Now look here,” said the captain. “You’ve run me to ground; here I am; well then — out with it; what is it?”

“That’s you, Bill,” said Black Dog. “You’re in the right of it, Billy. I’ll have a glass of rum from this dear child I’ve taken such a liking to, and we’ll sit down, if you please, and talk straight, like old shipmates.”

When I came back with the rum, the two were already seated on either side of the captain’s breakfast — Black Dog next the door, sitting sideways so as to keep one eye on his old shipmate and one, I thought, on his line of retreat.
He told me to go out and leave the door standing wide. “None of your keyholes for me, sonny,” he said; and I left the two of them together and slipped back to the bar.
For a long time, though I certainly did my best to listen, I could make out nothing but a low murmur; but at last the voices rose, and I could pick up a word or two, mostly oaths, from the captain.
“No, no, no, no — and there’s an end of it!” he cried once; and again, “If it comes to swinging, let all swing, says I.”

Then all at once came a great burst of oaths and other noise — chair and table went over together, a clash of steel followed, then a cry of pain, and the next moment I saw Black Dog in full flight and the captain hard after him, both with drawn cutlasses, Black Dog streaming blood from the left shoulder. Right at the door the captain aimed one last tremendous slash, which would surely have split him to the backbone had it not caught on the big signboard of the Admiral Benbow. You can see the notch on the lower edge of the frame to this day.

That blow ended the fight. Once out on the road, Black Dog, wound and all, showed a wonderful clean pair of heels and was over the brow of the hill in half a minute. The captain, for his part, stood staring at the signboard like a man dazed. Then he passed his hand over his eyes again and again, and at last turned back indoors.
“Jim,” said he, “rum.” And as he spoke he swayed a little, and caught himself with one hand against the wall.
“Are you hurt?” cried I.
“Rum,” he said again. “I must get away from here. Rum! Rum!”

I ran for it, but I was so shaken by all that had happened that I broke a glass and jammed the tap, and while I was still fumbling I heard a heavy fall in the parlour, and running in, found the captain stretched full length on the floor. At the same moment my mother, alarmed by the shouting and the fighting, came hurrying down to help. Between us we lifted his head. He was breathing very loud and hard, but his eyes were shut and his face a dreadful colour.
“Dear, deary me,” cried my mother, “what a disgrace on the house — and your poor father lying sick upstairs!”

Meanwhile we had no notion how to help the captain, nor any thought but that he had got his death-wound in the scuffle with the stranger. I fetched the rum, sure enough, and tried to get it down his throat, but his teeth were clenched and his jaws as strong as iron. It was a blessed relief when the door opened and Doctor Livesey came in, on his visit to my father.
“Oh, doctor,” we cried, “what are we to do? Where is the man hurt?”

“Hurt? Rubbish!” said the doctor. “No more hurt than you or I. The man has had a stroke, just as I warned him. Now, Mrs. Hawkins, run up to your husband and, if you can, tell him nothing of this. For my part, I must do my best to save this fellow’s three-times-worthless life. Jim, fetch me a basin.”

When I got back with the basin the doctor had already slit the captain’s sleeve and laid bare his great sinewy arm, tattooed in several places. “Here’s luck,” “A fair wind,” and “Billy Bones his fancy” were lettered very neat and clear along the forearm; and up near the shoulder was a sketch of a gallows with a man hanging from it — done, I thought, with great spirit.

“Prophetic,” said the doctor, touching the picture with his finger. “And now, Master Billy Bones — if that is your name — we’ll have a look at the colour of your blood. Jim,” he said, “are you afraid of blood?”
“No, sir,” said I.
“Well then,” said he, “you hold the basin.” And with that he took his lancet and opened a vein.

A great deal of blood was taken before the captain opened his eyes and looked round him, bleary. First he made out the doctor, with an unmistakable scowl; then his eye fell on me, and he looked relieved. But all at once his colour changed, and he struggled to sit up, crying, “Where’s Black Dog?”

“There is no Black Dog here,” said the doctor, “except the one on your own back. You have been drinking rum, and you have had a stroke, exactly as I told you; and I have just this minute, much against my will, hauled you headfirst out of the grave. Now, Mr. Bones—”
“That’s not my name,” he broke in.

“Much I care,” said the doctor. “It’s the name of a buccaneer I’ve heard of, and I shall call you by it for short. Here is what I have to say to you: one glass of rum won’t kill you, but if you take one you’ll take another, and another, and I stake my wig that if you don’t break off short you’ll die — do you understand? Die. And go to your own place, like the man in the Bible. Come now, make the effort. I’ll help you to your bed this once.”
Between us, with no end of trouble, we got him upstairs and laid him on his bed, where his head fell back on the pillow as if he were near to fainting.
“Now, mind you,” said the doctor, “I clear my conscience — the name of rum, for you, is death.”
And with that he set off to see my father, drawing me along by the arm.

“This is nothing,” he said the moment he had shut the door. “I have drawn blood enough to keep him quiet a while; he should lie a week where he is — that is best for him and for you — but another stroke would settle him.”

chapters.title: The Black Spot
paragraphs: About noon I came to the captain’s door with some cooling drinks and his medicine. He was lying much as we had left him, only propped a little higher, and he looked both weak and worked-up.

“Jim,” he said, “you’re the only one here worth anything, and you know I’ve always been good to you. Never a month but I gave you your silver fourpenny. And now, mate, you see I’m pretty low, and deserted by all; so, Jim, you’ll bring me one mug of rum — won’t you, matey?”
“The doctor—” I began.

But he broke in, cursing the doctor in a feeble voice but heartily. “Doctors is all swabs,” he said; “and that one there — what does he know about seafaring men? I’ve been in places hot as pitch, with mates dropping round me of Yellow Jack, and the good land heaving like the sea with earthquakes — what does the doctor know of country like that? I lived on rum, I tell you. It’s been meat and drink to me, and man and wife besides; and if I can’t have my rum now I’m a poor old hulk on a lee shore. My blood’ll be on you, Jim, and on that swab of a doctor.” And he ran on cursing a while. “Look, Jim, how my fingers won’t keep still,” he went on, pleading now. “I can’t hold ’em steady, not I. I’ve not had a drop this whole blessed day. That doctor’s a fool, I tell you. If I don’t get a dram of rum, Jim, I’ll have the horrors — I’ve seen some of ’em already. I saw old Flint, there in the corner behind you, plain as print; and if I get the horrors, I’m a man that’s lived rough, and I’ll raise Cain. Your own doctor said one glass wouldn’t hurt me. I’ll give you a golden guinea for a mug, Jim.”

He was growing more and more excited, and it frightened me for my father, who was very low that day and needed quiet; besides, the doctor’s words, now thrown back at him, had reassured me, and I was rather offended at being offered a bribe.
“I want no money of yours,” said I, “only what you owe my father. I’ll bring you one glass, and not another.”
When I brought it to him he snatched it greedily and drank it off.
“Aye, aye,” said he, “that’s a sight better, sure enough. And now, matey, did that doctor say how long I’m to lie here in this old berth?”
“A week at least,” said I.

“Thunder!” he cried. “A week! I can’t do that — they’d have the black spot on me by then. The lubbers are casting about to get word of me this very minute — lubbers that couldn’t keep what they had, and now want to grab what is another man’s. Is that seamanly behaviour, now, I ask you? But I’m a saving soul. I never wasted good money of mine, nor lost it either; and I’ll trick ’em again. I’m not afraid of ’em. I’ll shake out another reef, matey, and leave ’em standing.”

As he spoke he had hauled himself up off the bed with great difficulty, gripping my shoulder so hard I nearly cried out, and dragging his legs like dead weight. His words, bold as they were in meaning, made a sad contrast with the feeble voice that carried them. He paused once he had got himself sitting on the edge.
“That doctor’s done for me,” he muttered. “My ears are singing. Lay me back.”
Before I could do much to help, he had dropped back to where he had been, and lay a while in silence.
“Jim,” he said at length, “you saw that seafaring man today?”
“Black Dog?” I asked.

“Ah — Black Dog,” said he. “He’s a bad one; but there’s worse behind him that put him on. Now, if I can’t get clear no way, and they tip me the black spot, mind you — it’s my old sea-chest they’re after. You get on a horse — you can ride, can’t you? Well then, you get on a horse and go to — yes, I will! — to that everlasting swab of a doctor, and tell him to pipe all hands, magistrates and such, and he’ll lay ’em aboard at the Admiral Benbow — all old Flint’s crew, every man and boy of ’em that’s left. I was first mate, I was — old Flint’s first mate — and I’m the only one as knows the place. He gave it me at Savannah, when he lay a-dying, like as I might now, you see. But you’ll not breathe a word unless they tip me the black spot, or unless you see that Black Dog again, or a seafaring man with one leg, Jim — him above all.”
“But what is the black spot, captain?” I asked.
“A summons, mate. I’ll tell you if they bring it. But you keep your weather-eye open, Jim, and I’ll share with you, fair halves, upon my honour.”

He rambled on a little longer, his voice growing weaker; but soon after I had given him his medicine — which he took like a child, with the remark, “If ever a sailor needed drugs, it’s me” — he fell at last into a heavy, swoon-like sleep, and I left him so. What I should have done if all had gone well I do not know. Most likely I should have told the doctor the whole story, for I was in mortal fear the captain might regret his confidences and make an end of me. But as it fell out, my poor father died quite suddenly that evening, and that pushed everything else aside. Our natural grief, the neighbours’ visits, the arranging of the funeral, and all the inn’s work to be carried on in the meantime kept me so busy that I had scarcely time to think of the captain, far less to be afraid of him.

He did get downstairs the next morning, to be sure, and ate his meals as usual, though little, and took, I am afraid, more than his share of rum, helping himself at the bar, scowling and snorting, with nobody daring to cross him. The night before the funeral he was as drunk as ever, and it was shocking, in that house of mourning, to hear him bawling out his ugly old sea-song; but weak as he was, we all went in fear of him, and the doctor had been called away suddenly to a case many miles off and never came near the house after my father’s death. I have said the captain was weak, and indeed he seemed to grow weaker rather than mend. He hauled himself up and down stairs, and went from the parlour to the bar and back, and now and then put his nose out of doors to smell the sea, holding to the walls for support as he went and breathing hard and fast like a man climbing a steep hill. He never spoke to me directly, and it is my belief he had as good as forgotten what he had confided; but his temper was flightier, and — allowing for his bodily weakness — more violent than ever. He had an alarming new way, when drunk, of drawing his cutlass and laying it bare on the table before him. Yet for all that, he took less notice of people, and seemed shut up in his own thoughts, and rather wandering. Once, for instance, to our great surprise, he struck up a different tune — a kind of country love-song he must have learned in his youth, before he took to the sea.

So things went until, the day after the funeral — about three o’clock of a bitter, foggy, frosty afternoon — I was standing a moment at the door, full of sad thoughts of my father, when I saw someone coming slowly along the road. He was plainly blind, for he tapped ahead of him with a stick and wore a great green shade over his eyes and nose; and he was bent, as if with age or weakness, and wrapped in a huge old tattered sea-cloak with a hood that made him look positively deformed. I never in my life saw a more dreadful-looking figure. He stopped a little short of the inn and, raising his voice in an odd sing-song, called out to the air in front of him: “Will any kind friend tell a poor blind man, who has lost the precious sight of his eyes in the gracious defence of his native country, England — and God bless King George! — where, or in what part of the country, he may now be?”
“This is the Admiral Benbow, at Black Hill Cove, my good man,” I told him.
“I hear a voice,” said he — “a young one. Give me your hand, my kind young friend, and lead me inside.”

I held out my hand, and the horrible, soft-spoken, eyeless creature gripped it in a moment like a vice. I was so startled that I tried to pull away, but with one motion of his arm the blind man dragged me close.
“Now, boy,” said he, “take me in to the captain.”
“Sir,” said I, “upon my word I dare not.”
“Oh,” he sneered, “that’s it, is it? Take me in straight, or I’ll break your arm.”
And as he spoke he gave it a wrench that made me cry out.
“Sir,” said I, “it is for your own sake. The captain is not what he used to be. He sits with a drawn cutlass. Another gentleman—”

“Come, now — march,” he cut in; and I never heard a voice so cruel and cold and ugly as that blind man’s. It cowed me more than the pain, and I began to obey him at once, walking straight in at the door and toward the parlour, where our sick old buccaneer sat, dazed with rum. The blind man clung to me, gripping me in one iron fist and leaning more of his weight on me than I could well carry. “Lead me straight up to him, and when I’m in sight, call out, ‘Here’s a friend for you, Bill.’ If you don’t, I’ll do this” — and he gave me a twist that I thought would have made me faint. Between this and that, I was so utterly terrified of the blind beggar that I forgot my dread of the captain, and as I opened the parlour door I called out the words he had ordered, in a trembling voice.

The poor captain looked up, and at one glance the rum went clean out of him and left him staring sober. His face showed not so much terror as mortal sickness. He made a movement to rise, but I do not believe he had the strength left in his body.

“Stay where you are, Bill,” said the beggar. “Blind I may be, but I can hear a finger stir. Business is business. Put out your left hand. Boy — take him by the wrist and bring his left hand over to my right.”
We both obeyed him to the letter, and I saw him pass something from the hollow of the hand that held his stick into the captain’s palm, which closed on it at once.

“And now that’s done,” said the blind man; and with the words he suddenly let go of me and, with astonishing speed and sureness, skipped out of the parlour and into the road, where, as I still stood frozen, I could hear his stick go tap-tap-tapping off into the distance.

It was some time before either of us came to his senses; but at last, and about at the same moment, I let go his wrist, which I was still holding, and he drew in his hand and looked sharply at the palm.
“Ten o’clock!” he cried. “Six hours — we’ll beat ’em yet,” and he sprang to his feet.
Even as he did, he reeled, put his hand to his throat, stood swaying a moment, and then, with an odd sound, fell his whole height face-first to the floor.

I ran to him at once, calling for my mother. But all haste was useless. The captain had been struck dead by a thundering stroke. It is a strange thing to account for, since I had certainly never liked the man — though of late I had begun to pity him — but the moment I saw he was dead, I burst into a flood of tears. It was the second death I had known, and the grief of the first was still fresh in my heart.
